source: The Chandrasekhar Limit
Electrons moving near light speed can hold up at most about 1.4 solar masses.
Students think the limit applies to the whole star rather than to its core or remnant.

In 1930, on a ship from India to England, the 19-year-old Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar added special relativity to the theory of white-dwarf sizes and found that there is a largest possible white dwarf. The result earned him a share of the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.

As a white dwarf gains mass and shrinks, its electrons are squeezed to higher momenta. Once $p_F \gtrsim m_ec$, the fastest electrons move at nearly $c$ instead of $p/m_e$. The pressure, roughly $n_e \times p_F \times v$, then grows as $n_e \times n_e^{1/3} \times c$, so $P \propto \rho^{4/3}$ instead of $\rho^{5/3}$. Compare with gravity: $P \propto (M/R^3)^{4/3} = M^{4/3}/R^4$, while gravity needs $M^2/R^4$. Both go as $1/R^4$, so shrinking no longer helps. Only one mass balances; above it, gravity wins at every radius and the star collapses. Dimensional analysis gives that mass from the constants alone: $$M \sim \left(\frac{\hbar c}{G}\right)^{3/2}\frac{1}{(\mu_em_p)^2} \approx 0.5\,M_\odot \text{ for } \mu_e = 2,$$ and the full calculation multiplies it by about 3.1.

The Chandrasekhar limit is $M_{\text{Ch}} \approx 5.83\,M_\odot/\mu_e^2$, about $1.4\,M_\odot$ for carbon, oxygen or helium ($\mu_e = 2$). No white dwarf, and no stellar core supported by electron degeneracy, can be heavier.
Worked examples
Evaluate $(\hbar c/G)^{3/2}/(\mu_em_p)^2$ for $\mu_e = 2$ ($\hbar c = 3.16 \times 10^{-26}$ J·m).
The dimensional estimate
About $0.46\,M_\odot$; times 3.1 gives about $1.4\,M_\odot$.
$(2m_p)^2 = 1.12 \times 10^{-53}$ kg², so the ratio is $9.2 \times 10^{29}$ kg.
At what density does $p_F = m_ec$ for $\mu_e = 2$?
When do the electrons become relativistic?
About $2 \times 10^{9}$ kg/m³, a few times the mean density of a typical white dwarf and about its central density. In heavier white dwarfs, the central electrons are strongly relativistic.
$n_e = \dfrac{1}{3\pi^2}\left(\dfrac{m_ec}{\hbar}\right)^3 = \dfrac{(2.59 \times 10^{12})^3}{29.6} = 5.9 \times 10^{35}$ m⁻³.
$\rho = 2m_pn_e$.
What is the limit for a core of iron-56 ($Z = 26$)?
An iron core
About $1.26\,M_\odot$ in this simple model: iron has fewer electrons per nucleon, so it can support less.

Applying the limit to the whole star. A star of 6 solar masses can still end as a white dwarf: it sheds most of its mass in winds and a planetary nebula, and only its core, below the limit, remains. The limit concerns the mass supported by degenerate electrons: a white dwarf, or the core inside a massive star. When a massive star's iron core grows past it, the core collapses (next topic). A white dwarf in a binary that gains matter until it nears the limit can explode as a type Ia supernova.

The 5.83 comes from solving the structure equations exactly for fully relativistic electrons. Detailed models with the electrons' finite mass and other small effects give about $1.4\,M_\odot$ for carbon–oxygen white dwarfs, and no white dwarf heavier than that has been found.
